passages.happening:
Paul turns suddenly on someone listening. “You, therefore, have no excuse, you who pass judgment on another. For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself, because you who pass judgment do the same things” (verse 1).

God's judgment against such things is true (verse 2). So, Paul asks, “when you, O man, pass judgment on others, yet do the same things, do you think you will escape God’s judgment?” (verse 3).

Or do you look down on God's great kindness, patience and forbearance, “not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” (verse 4). A hard heart that will not turn, he warns, is “storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Imagine the room. The end of chapter 1 has been read aloud: idols, lust, envy, murder, gossip. Everyone has been nodding. Then the reader turns, and the letter says ‘you’.

Paul writes here in a teaching style his hearers knew. A teacher would speak to an imagined listener, ‘O man’, put that person's questions into words, and answer them. The ‘you’ is not one person in Rome. It is anyone who agreed with chapter 1 and felt safe.

Who did Paul mainly have in mind? Many readers think he is already speaking to a Jewish listener, who would have agreed with every word against Gentile idols, and whom he names openly in verse 17. Others think he means any moral person, Jew or Gentile, who judges others. Either way, the effect is the same: no one gets to stand outside chapter 1 and point in.

‘Kindness’ here is the Greek chrēstotēs, goodness that is generous. God's patience is not a sign that he does not care about wrong. It is room he gives people to turn. ‘Repentance’ means a turning of mind and life back to God.
passages.ot:
The prophets said the same thing to Israel. When King David condemned the rich man in Nathan's story, Nathan answered, “You are that man” (2 Samuel 12:7). David had judged himself.

God's patience is an old theme. When he passed before Moses he called himself “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). The prophet Joel called Israel to return because the LORD is “gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion” (Joel 2:13).

The ‘day of wrath’ is a phrase of the prophets: Zephaniah called the day of the LORD “a day of wrath” (Zephaniah 1:15).
passages.hard: Does God's patience mean he will not judge? Paul says the reverse. God's kindness is meant to lead people to turn, and patience refused does not cancel judgment; it stores it up. That is a hard word, and Paul means it as a warning, not a threat to enjoy. He is speaking to people who were sure they were on the right side. The danger he names is not only the sinner who knows he is lost. It is the person who judges others and never thinks to look at himself.
passages.asks: Paul catches the reader who agreed too quickly with chapter 1. Ask where you have been quick to judge others for things you excuse in yourself. Then ask what God's patience with you has been for. Has it made you careless, or has it drawn you to turn back to him?

passages.happening:
God “will repay each one according to his deeds” (verse 6). Paul spells it out in two lines and then repeats them.

To those who keep on doing good and seek glory, honour and immortality, God will give eternal life (verse 7). For those who are self-seeking, who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger (verse 8).

There will be trouble and distress for everyone who does evil, “first for the Jew, then for the Greek” (verse 9); but glory, honour and peace for everyone who does good, “first for the Jew, then for the Greek” (verse 10).

“For God does not show favoritism” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The passage is built like a mirror. It starts with God's fair judgment, moves to life and wrath, then wrath and life again, and ends with God's fairness. Hearers who listened carefully would catch the shape.

‘First for the Jew, then for the Greek’ has appeared before, about the gospel (1:16). Now it is used about judgment as well. Being first in God's promises also means being first in responsibility. Privilege does not mean protection.

‘Favoritism’ translates a Greek word that means, literally, ‘receiving the face’: judging by who a person is rather than by what they have done. In the ancient world, as now, judges were often swayed by rank, wealth or family. Paul says God is not.

Notice the people who are given eternal life: those who ‘by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality’ (verse 7). They are not proud of themselves. They are seeking something from God that they do not have.
passages.ot:
Paul's first line is a quotation. The Psalms say to God, “For You will repay each man according to his deeds” (Psalm 62:12), and Proverbs asks, “Will He not repay a man according to his deeds?” (Proverbs 24:12).

The law of Moses called God “the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17), and it commanded Israel's judges to be the same.
passages.hard:
Does Romans 2 teach that people are saved by their good deeds? Verse 7 promises eternal life to those who persist in doing good, and verse 13 says “the doers of the law who will be declared righteous”. Yet in 3:20 and 3:28 Paul says no one is justified by works of the law. How do these fit?

Readers give three main answers. First, many in the Reformation tradition say Paul is stating the law's standard: if anyone truly did good, they would be justified, but chapter 3 shows that no one does. Second, others say Paul is describing believers, Jew and Gentile, whose lives are changed by the Spirit so that they truly do what the law asks. Third, many say that the final judgment really does look at what people have done, and that for believers those deeds are the fruit and evidence of faith, not its ground. Many readers combine the second and the third.

All agree on two things. Paul is not contradicting his teaching that people are set right with God by grace through faith. And he takes how people live seriously. Grace never makes obedience unimportant.
passages.asks: God does not show favouritism. Ask whether you expect him to, for you, for your family, your church or your side. Then ask what ‘doing good’ with ‘perseverance’ would look like in your ordinary week, not as a way to earn God's favour but as the shape of a life that is seeking him.

passages.t: The law written on the heart
passages.happening:
Paul explains how God judges people with the law and without it. All who sin without the law will perish without the law, and all who sin under the law will be judged by the law (verse 12). “For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous” (verse 13).

Then he turns to Gentiles. When Gentiles, who do not have the law, “do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves” (verse 14). “So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them” (verse 15).

This will come out “on the day when God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
‘The law’ here means the law God gave Israel through Moses. Jews had it, written down, read aloud in the synagogue every Sabbath. Gentiles did not.

‘Hearers of the law’ is an exact picture. Most people then did not own books. They heard the law read aloud. Paul says hearing it is not enough. What matters is doing it.

Greek thinkers also spoke of a law of nature, a sense of right and wrong found in human beings as such. Paul's hearers would have known the idea. Paul uses it, but places it inside the Bible's story: what God wrote on stone for Israel, he has also, in some measure, written on every human heart.

‘Conscience’ is the Greek suneidēsis, the inner witness that judges our own actions. Paul says it sometimes accuses and sometimes defends. Everyone knows that experience. Elsewhere he says conscience can be weak or damaged (1 Corinthians 8:7), so it is a real guide, but not the final judge. God is.

‘Through Christ Jesus’. The judge on the last day, Paul says, is Jesus. That is part of his gospel.
passages.ot:
Paul's picture of a law ‘written on their hearts’ echoes the promise of a new covenant in Jeremiah: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

Ezekiel promised the same: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26), and “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).

The Psalms already knew that God sees what is hidden: “Search me, O God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Paul says that on the last day the secrets will be judged.
passages.hard:
Who are the Gentiles who ‘do by nature what the law requires’ (verse 14)? Readers answer in two main ways.

Some say Paul means ordinary Gentiles, people of any nation, who do some good by conscience without having God's law. On this reading, Paul shows that everyone has a law to answer to, so that everyone is accountable, and the argument heads toward “all have sinned” (3:23). Conscience shows the law is written on the heart. It does not show that anyone keeps it well enough to be saved.

Others say Paul means Gentile Christians. They hear in ‘written on their hearts’ the new covenant of Jeremiah 31, fulfilled by the Spirit, and they read verse 29 the same way.

Does this passage say what happens to people who never heard of Jesus? It says that God judges people by the light they had, and that no one is judged for a law they never received. It does not say how, or whether, those who never heard are saved through Christ. Faithful Christians answer that question in more than one way. The site's Honest Answer, ‘What about those who never heard of Jesus?’, sets out the main views with care.
passages.asks: Paul says it is not hearing that counts, but doing. Ask how much of what you know about God's will you actually do. Then think about your conscience: when does it accuse you, and when do you argue it down? And remember who the judge is. The one who knows every secret is the one who died for sinners.

passages.happening:
Now Paul names the listener he has been speaking to. “Now you, if you call yourself a Jew; if you rely on the law and boast in God” (verse 17); if you know God's will and approve what is best because you are taught by the law (verse 18); if you are sure you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, a teacher of the foolish and of children, because you have in the law the very shape of knowledge and truth (verses 19-20).

Then come the questions. “you, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (verse 21). “You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?” (verse 22). “You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?” (verse 23).

And he ends with Scripture: “God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The list of privileges in verses 17 to 20 is not mockery. Every item was true. Israel did have God's law. Israel was called to be a light to the nations. Jewish communities across the empire taught one God in a world of idols, and many Gentiles admired their way of life and came to the synagogue to learn. Paul, once a Pharisee, had been just such a teacher.

His point is that having the truth is not the same as living it. The questions are sharp because they are about the very things a teacher teaches.

‘Do you rob temples?’ has puzzled readers. Jews hated idols and were forbidden to profit from the things of pagan temples (Deuteronomy 7:25-26). Paul may mean that some made money from goods taken from such temples, or he may use the phrase more widely for treating holy things as cheap. It is not certain what he had in mind.

This passage must be read carefully. Paul is a Jew speaking to a fellow Jew, in the manner of Israel's own prophets, who said far harder things to their people and were not their enemies. He is not making a charge against the Jewish people. His point applies to every person who knows the truth and teaches it, including every Christian teacher. The note below explains why it must never be used against the Jewish people.
passages.ot:
Israel's calling is in Isaiah: “I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations” (Isaiah 42:6).

The questions about stealing and adultery come from the Ten Commandments: “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15) and “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14).

Verse 24 quotes Isaiah 52:5. There God says that because his people have been carried off and ruled by others, “My name is blasphemed continually all day long” (Isaiah 52:5). Paul follows the Greek translation of Isaiah, which adds ‘among the Gentiles’ and ‘because of you’. Ezekiel says something close: wherever Israel went among the nations, “they profaned My holy name” (Ezekiel 36:20).
passages.hard:
How should these words be read? First, see who is speaking, and to whom. Paul is a Jew, “a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin” (11:1). He speaks to an imagined Jewish teacher as one of his own people, the way Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel spoke to theirs. He does not say Jews are worse than others. In chapter 1 he has just said the same kind of thing about Gentiles, and in chapter 3 he will say that all, Jew and Gentile alike, are under sin.

For centuries many Christians used words like these to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. This site rejects it. In Romans itself Paul grieves for his people (9:2), insists that God has not rejected them (11:1), and warns Gentile believers not to be proud (11:18-20). The questions of verses 21 to 23 belong to every Christian teacher, preacher and parent who has said one thing and done another.
passages.asks: Paul asks the teacher, ‘do you not teach yourself?’ If you teach, lead, preach or parent, put the question to yourself. Which of the things you tell others to do do you not do? And ask how people outside the church think of God because of how you live.

passages.happening:
Circumcision has value, Paul says, if you keep the law. But if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision (verse 25).

And the reverse: if a man who is not circumcised keeps the law's requirements, “will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?” (verse 26). The one who keeps the law without being circumcised will condemn the one who has the written code and circumcision and still breaks the law (verse 27).

“A man is not a Jew because he is one outwardly, nor is circumcision only outward and physical” (verse 28). “No, a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code. Such a man’s praise does not come from men, but from God” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17). In the Roman world it was the chief mark of being Jewish. Many Greeks and Romans found it strange. For a Gentile man to be circumcised was to become a Jew. So Paul's words here would have struck deep.

Paul does not say circumcision is worthless. In the next verses he says the Jew's advantage is great, “Much in every way” (3:2). He says that the outward sign without the inward reality is not enough before God.

‘By the Spirit, not by the written code’. The ‘written code’ is the law as letters on a page. Paul sets against it the work of God's Spirit inside a person. He will say more about this in chapters 7 and 8.

There is a wordplay here for those who knew Hebrew. The name Judah, from which the word ‘Jew’ comes, is linked in Genesis to praise: when Judah was born, Leah said, “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35). A true Jew, Paul says, is one whose praise comes from God.
passages.ot:
Paul did not invent the idea of a circumcised heart. Moses told Israel, “Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more” (Deuteronomy 10:16). And he promised that God himself would do it: “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

Jeremiah pressed the same call: “remove the foreskins of your hearts, O men of Judah and people of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 4:4). He warned of a day when God would punish those “who are circumcised yet uncircumcised” (Jeremiah 9:25).

The promise of the Spirit inside God's people comes from Ezekiel: “I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27).
passages.hard: Is Paul saying that Gentile Christians have replaced the Jewish people? No. He is saying what Moses and Jeremiah said: that the outward sign must be matched by a heart turned to God, and that God himself promised to do this inner work. Christians do read verses 26 to 29 in different ways: some see here Gentile believers who have received the Spirit, others see a principle that holds for anyone. But Paul goes straight on to ask, ‘What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew?’ and answers, “Much in every way” (3:2). In chapters 9 to 11 he insists that God's call to Israel stands. This passage does not cancel that.
passages.asks: Paul says real faith is ‘a matter of the heart’. Ask whether your faith lives mostly in outward things: attending, belonging, being known as a Christian. Those things have value, but they are not the heart. And ask whose praise you are living for. Paul says the true believer's praise ‘does not come from men, but from God’.
